full_citation: R. Verma, D. Barrejon, E. Nalisnick, 'Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts: Consistent Surrogate Losses, Confidence Calibration, and Conformal Ensembles', Proc. 26th Int. Conf. on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), PMLR 206, pp. 11415-11434, 2023.
discovery_source: Proposal reference [60]; re-verified via PMLR proceedings page
research_problem: Statistical foundations of deferring a prediction to one of several differentiated human experts: consistent surrogate losses, calibration, expert ensembling.
unit_of_decision: One classification instance x
human_role: Decision maker of last resort for deferred instances
when_human_is_involved: At inference, when the learned deferral rule selects deferral for instance x
who_is_selected: One of J named experts, or a conformal-inference-selected subset of experts
selection_signal: Estimated P(m_j = y | x) per expert j, i.e. instance-conditional expert correctness, plus model confidence
competence_modelled: YES - explicitly, and conditioned on the specific instance x, not an aggregate per-expert score
judgment_representation: The expert's output is a class label consumed as the system decision; no record object
reuse_supported: NO - the deferred label is a one-shot decision
evaluation_type: Offline benchmark experiments with simulated and human-derived expert labels
dataset: Galaxy morphology classification, skin lesion classification, hate speech classification
participants: No live human participants; expert labels drawn from existing annotations
baseline: Single-expert L2D surrogates (Mozannar and Sontag 2020; Verma and Nalisnick 2022)
metrics: System accuracy and calibration error at varying deferral rates
main_result: Two consistent multi-expert surrogates derived; the softmax parameterisation propagates mis-calibration between expert estimates while the one-vs-all parameterisation does not; conformal selection of an expert subset is proposed.
exact_gap_effect: Refutes the specific wording that multi-expert deferral conditions only on an aggregate competence profile over a task distribution. Instance-conditional per-expert competence must be conceded. GAP-1 survives only as the competence-AND-authority conjunction plus the claim-level unit and budgeted evaluation.
limitations: Requires per-expert ground-truth outcome labels; fixed known expert panel; single true label per instance, so no representation of several defensible readings; no attention-budget or selective-risk evaluation of the routing decision.
verified_source: PMLR v206 proceedings page; abstract quoted verbatim; page range matches proposal reference [60]

full_citation: A. Mao, C. Mohri, M. Mohri, Y. Zhong, 'Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts', Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36, 2023.
discovery_source: Proposal reference [61]; re-verified via NeurIPS proceedings
research_problem: Two-stage learning to defer where a predictor is fixed first and a deferral rule then routes among multiple experts, with consistency guarantees.
unit_of_decision: One prediction instance
human_role: One of several experts who may receive the instance
when_human_is_involved: At inference, on deferral
selection_signal: Expert-specific cost and accuracy, conditioned on the instance
judgment_representation: Expert prediction consumed as the decision; no record object
evaluation_type: Theoretical (realizable H-consistency bounds) with supporting experiments
metrics: Deferral loss, H-consistency bounds, accuracy-cost trade-off
main_result: Establishes realizable H-consistency for two-stage multi-expert deferral and derives corresponding surrogate losses.
exact_gap_effect: Reinforces G1-01. Confirms that routing among differentiated experts, architecturally separated from the base predictor, is established prior art.
limitations: Expert differentiation by cost and accuracy only; no authority, scope or eligibility; label-supervised.
verified_source: NeurIPS 2023 proceedings record (authors, title, venue, year). Page range 3578-3606 in reference [61] NOT independently confirmed.

full_citation: N. Russell, W. M. P. van der Aalst, A. H. M. ter Hofstede, D. Edmond, 'Workflow Resource Patterns: Identification, Representation and Tool Support', Advanced Information Systems Engineering (CAiSE 2005), LNCS 3520, pp. 216-232, 2005.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search mandated by proposal Section 2.6; web search plus Springer record
research_problem: The resource perspective of workflow had been neglected relative to control flow; the paper identifies and formalises the patterns by which work items are distributed to and executed by participants.
unit_of_decision: One work item (an activity instance in a running process case)
human_role: Participant who is offered, allocated or required to execute the work item
when_human_is_involved: At work-item creation, offer, allocation and start, i.e. by design at every distribution point
who_is_selected: A participant or set of participants resolved against an organisational model
selection_signal: Pattern-dependent: role membership, declared capability, organisational position, execution history, or prior familiarity with the case
competence_modelled: PARTIAL - Capability-Based Distribution matches DECLARED capability attributes; competence is not assessed from evidence
authority_modelled: YES - the Authorisation pattern plus Separation of Duties and Binding of Duties constrain who MAY execute the item
authority_distinct_from_competence: YES - capability-based distribution and authorisation are separate, independently specifiable patterns in the same catalogue
judgment_representation: Work-item state transitions and execution records; not a judgment record
scope_captured: PARTIAL - the constraint applies to the specified activity type
provenance: PARTIAL - work-item execution history is retained
revocation: PARTIAL - work items can be deallocated or reoffered
reuse_supported: PARTIAL - History-Based Distribution and Retain Familiar reuse past allocation outcomes
reuse_scope: Within the same process model and organisational model
authorization_checked: YES - by design, per work item
evaluation_type: Pattern identification and expressiveness assessment; tool support demonstration; no controlled outcome study
dataset: Commercial and open-source workflow product feature analysis
baseline: Comparative expressiveness of contemporary workflow systems
main_result: A catalogue of resource patterns including Role-Based and Capability-Based Distribution, Authorisation, Separation of Duties and History-Based Distribution, with an assessment of how poorly contemporary workflow systems supported them.
exact_gap_effect: The single closest structural match to GAP-1: one framework jointly represents a capability requirement and an authorisation constraint for a specific work item. GAP-1 must be narrowed from competence and authority are not represented together to ASSESSED, claim-specific competence has not been combined with authority in an evaluated routing policy.
limitations: Capability is declared, not assessed; unit is a work item with a defined completion criterion rather than a contested claim; a design vocabulary rather than an evaluated policy; no accuracy, budget or risk outcome reported.
verified_source: Crossref (DOI, pages 216-232, 2005) and Springer chapter record; workflowpatterns.com documentation for pattern names. NOTE: the Crossref container-title for this DOI is corrupted to an unrelated series.

full_citation: E. Bertino, E. Ferrari, V. Atluri, 'The specification and enforcement of authorization constraints in workflow management systems', ACM Transactions on Information and System Security 2(1), pp. 65-104, 1999.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search; Crossref bibliographic query
research_problem: How to specify and enforce, formally, which roles and users may execute which workflow tasks, including constraints spanning several tasks.
unit_of_decision: One workflow task assignment
human_role: Authorised or unauthorised executor of a task
when_human_is_involved: At task assignment and execution
who_is_selected: A user or role satisfying the authorisation constraints
selection_signal: Role membership and constraint satisfaction, including static and dynamic separation of duty and binding of duty
authority_modelled: YES - formally specified and algorithmically enforced
authority_distinct_from_competence: NA - only authority is modelled; competence is absent
judgment_representation: Task execution assignment records
scope_captured: YES - authorisation is scoped to specified tasks and constraint windows
provenance: PARTIAL - execution history is used for dynamic constraints
expiry: PARTIAL - dynamic constraints are evaluated relative to case state
revocation: PARTIAL - authorisations can be revoked in the model
evaluation_type: Formal - language definition, consistency results, and enforcement algorithm with complexity analysis
main_result: A logic-based constraint language and an enforcement algorithm assigning users and roles to workflow tasks while satisfying all declared authorisation constraints.
exact_gap_effect: Establishes authority modelling as mature prior art. The proposal must stop treating authority representation as unaddressed and instead argue that authority has never been conditioned on assessed competence for a contested interpretation.
limitations: No competence, skill or accuracy notion; authorisation is orthogonal to whether the authorised actor decides well; no contested-interpretation concept.

full_citation: L. Pufahl, F. Stiehle, S. Ihde, M. Weske, I. Weber, 'Resource allocation in business process executions - A systematic literature study', Information Systems, art. 102541, 2025.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search; web search then Crossref and OpenAlex verification
research_problem: What the literature on system-initiated resource allocation during business process execution actually does: which goals, inputs, criteria and methods it uses.
unit_of_decision: One process activity instance requiring a resource
human_role: Allocated resource
when_human_is_involved: At allocation time during process execution
who_is_selected: A resource satisfying allocation goals and constraints
selection_signal: Across 61 primary studies: resource and task attributes, process models and execution data
competence_modelled: PARTIAL across the corpus - resource capability and expertise appear as allocation attributes
authority_modelled: PARTIAL across the corpus - role constraints restrict which resources may perform an activity
authority_distinct_from_competence: PARTIAL - both appear as separate attribute families, but the review reports no approach evaluated on their joint, evidence-conditioned use
judgment_representation: not_applicable
evaluation_type: Systematic literature study
metrics: Classification coverage across allocation goals, inputs, criteria and methods
main_result: Reviewed approaches are predominantly rule-based and process-oriented, mostly 1-to-1 allocations; the review explicitly calls for consistent terminology, evidence-oriented allocation methods with greater adaptability, and comparative benchmarking to improve reproducibility.
exact_gap_effect: The decisive evidence that GAP-1 survives as NARROWED rather than refuted: the adjacent literature's own 2025 systematic review reports that its allocation methods are not evidence-oriented and are not comparatively benchmarked. Must replace the proposal's bare statement that BPM has not been searched.
limitations: A review, not an approach; scope is system-initiated allocation of process activities, so claim-level interpretive routing falls outside its unit of analysis; corpus ends 2023.
verified_source: Crossref (DOI, journal, 2025) and OpenAlex (authors, abstract, scope)

full_citation: M. Arias, E. Rojas, J. Munoz-Gama, M. Sepulveda, 'A Framework for Recommending Resource Allocation Based on Process Mining', Business Process Management Workshops, LNBIP, pp. 458-470.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search; Crossref bibliographic query
research_problem: How to recommend which resource should perform an activity, using evidence of past performance mined from event logs.
unit_of_decision: One process activity instance
human_role: Recommended resource
when_human_is_involved: At allocation decision time
who_is_selected: The resource ranked best for the activity by mined performance evidence
selection_signal: Historical performance metrics derived from event logs per resource and activity type
competence_modelled: YES - ASSESSED from event-log evidence rather than declared; the closest BPM analogue to assessed competence
authority_modelled: NO - not jointly modelled in the recommendation
judgment_representation: not_applicable
provenance: PARTIAL - recommendations trace to event-log evidence
reuse_supported: YES - past performance evidence is reused to inform later allocations
reuse_scope: Same process and activity types within the mined organisation
evaluation_type: Framework proposal with illustrative application
main_result: A framework that derives resource-allocation recommendations from process-mining evidence of historical resource performance.
exact_gap_effect: Closes the escape route that BPM has no assessed competence. GAP-1's residual must rest on the joint competence-and-authority decision, the claim-level unit, and budgeted evaluation.
limitations: Competence assessed at activity-type granularity, not for one contested claim; authority absent; recommends rather than governs; workshop-level evidence.

full_citation: C. Cabanillas, D. Knuplesch, M. Resinas, M. Reichert, J. Mendling, A. Ruiz-Cortes, 'RALph: A Graphical Notation for Resource Assignments in Business Processes', Advanced Information Systems Engineering (CAiSE 2015), LNCS, pp. 53-68, 2015.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search; Crossref bibliographic query
research_problem: How to express, graphically and formally, which resources may be assigned to a process activity.
unit_of_decision: One process activity
human_role: Assignable resource
when_human_is_involved: At design time (specification) and at resolution time
who_is_selected: Resources satisfying the assignment expression against an organisational model
selection_signal: Organisational position, role, declared capability, duty-separation and history conditions
authority_modelled: YES - organisational position and duty-separation conditions
authority_distinct_from_competence: YES - capability and position are separate expressible conditions
judgment_representation: not_applicable
scope_captured: YES - scoped to the specified activity
evaluation_type: Notation design plus formal semantics and expressiveness evaluation against the resource patterns
baseline: RAL and the workflow resource patterns
main_result: A graphical, formally grounded notation for resource assignment conditions, resolvable automatically against an organisational model.
exact_gap_effect: Confirms that jointly expressing capability and organisational authority is routine in BPM. Contributes to GAP-1's narrowing.
limitations: Declarative constraints over declared attributes; no assessed competence; no policy evaluation against outcomes.

full_citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 26(2).
venue: Official Journal of the European Union (binding regulation)
discovery_source: Adversarial search for authority-plus-competence conjunctions; verified against consolidated article text
research_problem: Obligations on deployers of high-risk AI systems, including the assignment of human oversight.
unit_of_decision: Assignment of the oversight duty for a high-risk AI system, at role level rather than claim level
human_role: Assigned human overseer
when_human_is_involved: Throughout deployment, as specified by the oversight measures
who_is_selected: Natural persons assigned by the deployer
selection_signal: Necessary competence, training and authority, plus necessary support
competence_modelled: YES - required as a normative precondition, with no assessment method specified
authority_modelled: YES - required as a normative precondition
authority_distinct_from_competence: YES - competence, training and authority are enumerated as distinct requirements in the same provision
judgment_representation: not_applicable
scope_captured: PARTIAL - scoped to the high-risk system deployed
contestability: PARTIAL - the Regulation provides complaint and explanation rights elsewhere
evaluation_type: Legal instrument - no empirical evaluation
main_result: Article 26(2): Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.
exact_gap_effect: Removes any claim that conjoining competence and authority is conceptually novel, since binding regulation already mandates it. Novelty must be relocated to operationalisation: a per-claim, evidence-conditioned, budgeted and evaluated routing policy. Simultaneously strengthens the practical motivation for Study 1.
limitations: States a requirement, not a mechanism. No per-claim selection procedure, no competence assessment method, no evaluation.
verified_source: Consolidated Article 26 text quoted verbatim. The candidate should re-verify against the EUR-Lex Official Journal text before citing.

full_citation: T. Clark, P. N. Ciccarese, C. A. Goble, 'Micropublications: a semantic model for claims, evidence, arguments and annotations in biomedical communications', Journal of Biomedical Semantics 5:28, 2014.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on claim-level records; Crossref and OpenAlex verification
research_problem: Scientific publications are defeasible arguments supported by data and methods, but the linear document form makes evidence unverifiable and citation chains unreliable; a machine-tractable claim-level model is needed.
unit_of_decision: One CLAIM, a single natural-language statement
human_role: Author or claimant, and challenger of others' claims
when_human_is_involved: At authoring, annotation, review and challenge
competence_modelled: NO - identity attribution only, no competence estimate
authority_distinct_from_competence: NO - neither is modelled as a decision right
judgment_representation: OWL 2 / RDF model: claim plus attribution plus supporting data, methods and materials plus the connecting argument plus discussion, challenges and opposition
rationale_captured: YES - the argument connecting evidence to the claim is explicit
scope_captured: NO - no validity scope on the claim
provenance: YES - claim provenance and evidence chains are first class
disagreement_preserved: YES - the model explicitly supports challenge and disagreement, and maximal forms include challenges brought forward or opposition
version_binding: PARTIAL - claims are individually identified and RDF-serialisable; no binding to a versioned target artefact
contestability: YES - challenge is a modelled relation between claims
reuse_supported: PARTIAL - claims are citable and machine-readable, so they can be referenced later
reuse_scope: Scholarly citation and annotation; no governed reuse decision
evaluation_type: Model specification with RDF examples and case studies; no controlled evaluation of capture cost or reconstructability
metrics: None reported - an expressiveness argument rather than measurement
main_result: A semantic model providing claims with attribution, evidence, methods, argument and retained challenge, serialisable in RDF with an OWL 2 vocabulary, presented as necessary where simpler statement-based models are insufficient for qualified, nuanced assertions.
exact_gap_effect: Directly narrows Section 2.4's claim that no record format combines reasoning-level content, retained disagreement and provenance at claim level - it does. GAP-2's residual reduces to validity scope, competence and authority, and a lifecycle that can lapse. Must be cited.
limitations: No scope, competence, authority, expiry, revocation or supersession; no evaluation of capture cost or blind reconstructability; biomedical scholarly-communication setting.
verified_source: Crossref (DOI, journal, article 28, 2014) and OpenAlex (authors, abstract)

full_citation: P. Groth, A. Gibson, J. Velterop, 'The anatomy of a nanopublication', Information Services and Use 30(1-2), pp. 51-56, 2010.
peer_review_status: Tier B - peer-reviewed journal (short position article)
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on claim-level records; Crossref verification
research_problem: How to publish and cite the smallest meaningful unit of scientific assertion so that it is machine-readable and individually attributable.
unit_of_decision: One assertion
human_role: Author and attributed source
when_human_is_involved: At publication
judgment_representation: Assertion plus provenance plus publication information, immutably identified
provenance: YES - provenance is a constitutive component
disagreement_preserved: NO - conflicting nanopublications may coexist but conflict is not modelled
version_binding: YES - immutable and individually identified, giving version-exact citability
revocation: PARTIAL - retraction is an ecosystem convention, not a modelled lifecycle state
supersession: PARTIAL - by publishing a superseding nanopublication, not by a modelled transition
evaluation_type: Conceptual specification; no empirical evaluation
main_result: Defines a nanopublication as an assertion together with its provenance and publication information, immutable and individually citable.
exact_gap_effect: Concedes version-exact, claim-level provenance as established prior art, narrowing GAP-2's version-binding element.
limitations: Factual assertions rather than governed human judgments; no rationale, scope, authority, competence or modelled lifecycle; short position article.

full_citation: J. Singh, J. Cobbe, C. Norval, 'Decision Provenance: Harnessing Data Flow for Accountable Systems', IEEE Access 7, pp. 6562-6574, 2019.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on decision-level provenance; Crossref verification
research_problem: How to make decisions taken by data-driven and interconnected systems inspectable and accountable, including across organisational boundaries.
unit_of_decision: One system decision
human_role: Accountable party, auditor, and data subject seeking redress
when_human_is_involved: After the decision, for audit, explanation and redress
judgment_representation: Provenance records of the data flows and processing steps that produced the decision
rationale_captured: PARTIAL - the causal pipeline is recorded, not human reasoning
version_binding: PARTIAL - pipeline versions can be recorded
contestability: PARTIAL - motivated by accountability and redress, but no modelled challenge relation
evaluation_type: Conceptual and legal analysis with system-design implications; no controlled evaluation
main_result: Argues for and frames decision provenance: applying provenance methods specifically to decision pipelines to support legal and organisational accountability.
exact_gap_effect: Occupies the conceptual space between PROV-DM [47] and SQ2, and is absent from the anchor set. Its omission weakens the claim that the step from provenance to governed decision records is unmade.
limitations: Records how a decision was produced; does not make a human judgment a reusable governed object with scope, authority or a lapse condition; no adjudication of conflicting qualified judgments.

full_citation: J. Doyle, 'A truth maintenance system', Artificial Intelligence 12(3), pp. 231-272, 1979.
discovery_source: Mandatory adjacent-literature target named in proposal Section 2.6; Crossref verification
research_problem: How a reasoning system should maintain a consistent set of beliefs when assumptions and justifications change, without recomputing everything.
unit_of_decision: One belief (assertion) in the belief store
human_role: not_applicable
when_human_is_involved: not_applicable
judgment_representation: Node with justifications recording which other beliefs support it
rationale_captured: PARTIAL - logical justification, not human rationale
scope_captured: PARTIAL - a belief holds only in contexts where its justification holds
provenance: YES - the justification structure is a dependency provenance record
disagreement_preserved: NO - the system drives to one consistent state
expiry: PARTIAL - a belief loses status when its justification lapses; the condition is logical, not temporal
revocation: YES - dependency-directed backtracking withdraws beliefs automatically when support is withdrawn
supersession: YES - beliefs are replaced when justifications change
validity_checked: YES - continuously, against current justification status
evaluation_type: Formal system design with worked examples
main_result: A system that records justifications for beliefs and automatically retracts beliefs whose support is withdrawn, via dependency-directed backtracking.
exact_gap_effect: Confirms the exposure the proposal itself declares. The consequence obliging an invalidated judgment to stop influencing decisions that Section 2.4 says provenance lacks is exactly what a TMS supplies. Section 2.4 must concede this and relocate its residual to human-authored, authority-bearing judgments.
limitations: Support is logical dependency, not an external validity condition such as a changed guideline or withdrawn mandate; no human agent, competence, authority, disagreement or human-readable rationale.

full_citation: J. de Kleer, 'An assumption-based TMS', Artificial Intelligence 28(2), pp. 127-162, 1986.
discovery_source: Mandatory adjacent-literature target named in proposal Section 2.6; Crossref verification
research_problem: How to reason simultaneously in multiple, mutually inconsistent contexts rather than maintaining a single consistent belief state.
unit_of_decision: One assertion, labelled with the assumption sets under which it holds
human_role: not_applicable
when_human_is_involved: not_applicable
judgment_representation: Node with a label of minimal assumption sets (environments) supporting it
scope_captured: YES - each assertion carries the assumption context in which it is valid
disagreement_preserved: YES - mutually inconsistent conclusions are maintained concurrently, each with its supporting context
contestability: PARTIAL - competing contexts coexist but there is no challenge procedure
evaluation_type: Formal system design with complexity discussion and worked examples
main_result: An assumption-based TMS that maintains all consistent contexts simultaneously, labelling each assertion with the minimal assumption sets under which it holds.
exact_gap_effect: Supplies retained disagreement combined with explicit scope-of-validity, formally, in 1986. Narrows two of GAP-2's elements simultaneously.
limitations: Assumptions are propositional, not organisational scope or authority; no human attribution, competence or mandate-based revocation.

full_citation: C. Gutierrez, C. A. Hurtado, A. Vaisman, 'Introducing Time into RDF', IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering 19(2), pp. 207-218, 2007.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on temporal validity and validity intervals; Crossref verification
research_problem: RDF has no standard way to state that an assertion holds only over a period of time; a temporal semantics and entailment regime is needed.
unit_of_decision: One RDF triple with a temporal label
human_role: not_applicable
when_human_is_involved: not_applicable
judgment_representation: Temporally labelled triple
version_binding: PARTIAL - temporal versions of a graph
expiry: YES - an assertion ceases to hold at the end of its validity interval, a lapse on a stated condition
reuse_supported: PARTIAL - temporal queries retrieve assertions valid at a stated time
evaluation_type: Formal - semantics, entailment and complexity results
main_result: A temporal extension of RDF with semantics and entailment, giving assertions explicit validity intervals.
exact_gap_effect: Engages SQ2's second stated refutation condition head-on, a lifecycle state able to lapse on a stated condition, and satisfies it under a time-only reading. The proposal must tighten that condition to a non-temporal, policy-or-evidence-keyed lapse, or concede the point.
limitations: The lapse condition is strictly a time interval; it cannot express lapse on guideline change, mandate withdrawal or challenge by a more authorised reviewer; no rationale, competence, authority or disagreement.

full_citation: A. Uma, T. Fornaciari, D. Hovy, S. Paun, B. Plank, M. Poesio, 'Learning from Disagreement: A Survey', Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 72, pp. 1385-1470, 2021.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on annotation disagreement; Crossref verification
research_problem: How to treat systematic disagreement among qualified annotators as signal rather than noise, and how to train and evaluate models accordingly.
unit_of_decision: One annotation item and its label distribution
human_role: Annotator whose judgment is retained rather than aggregated away
when_human_is_involved: At annotation time
competence_modelled: PARTIAL - annotator reliability models appear in the surveyed corpus
judgment_representation: Per-annotator labels or a soft label distribution rather than a single gold label
disagreement_preserved: YES - the central subject of the survey
reuse_supported: YES - as training and evaluation signal
evaluation_type: Survey of methods, datasets and evaluation practices
main_result: Surveys and systematises methods that learn from annotator disagreement, showing that aggregating to a single gold label destroys recoverable information.
exact_gap_effect: Section 2.4 currently rests the disagreement claim on a single 2015 AI Magazine article. Citing this survey removes an under-evidencing risk without weakening the gap, since none of the surveyed methods adjudicates to an authoritative verdict.
limitations: Concerns label distributions for model training; no per-judgment governed record, scope, authority or lifecycle; adjudication to a verdict is explicitly avoided rather than solved.

full_citation: A. MacLean, R. M. Young, V. M. E. Bellotti, T. P. Moran, 'Questions, Options, and Criteria: Elements of Design Space Analysis', Human-Computer Interaction 6(3-4), pp. 201-250, 1991.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on rationale capture; Crossref verification
research_problem: How to represent the reasoning behind a design so that the alternatives considered and the criteria applied remain available to later readers.
unit_of_decision: One design question
human_role: Designer who states questions, options and criteria
when_human_is_involved: During design deliberation and documentation
judgment_representation: Semi-formal QOC structure: questions, the options answering each, and the criteria assessing the options
rationale_captured: YES - including the alternatives not chosen and why
scope_captured: PARTIAL - scoped to the design question
disagreement_preserved: PARTIAL - competing options and conflicting criteria are retained, though not attributed to disagreeing people
contestability: PARTIAL - the structure invites re-argument but specifies no challenge procedure
reuse_supported: PARTIAL - the design space can be revisited
reuse_scope: Later design work on the same artefact
evaluation_type: Conceptual framework with worked design examples; no controlled study of capture cost or later reconstruction
baseline: Narrative design documentation and IBIS-style rationale
main_result: A representation of design rationale as questions, options and criteria, making the considered design space explicit and inspectable.

full_citation: T. Zimmermann, N. Nagappan, H. Gall, E. Giger, B. Murphy, 'Cross-project defect prediction: a large scale experiment on data vs. domain vs. process', Proc. 7th Joint Meeting of the European Software Engineering Conference and the ACM SIGSOFT Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering (ESEC/FSE 2009), pp. 91-100, 2009.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on transferable-versus-local failure attribution; Crossref verification
research_problem: When does a defect predictor built on one software project actually work on a different project, and which data, domain and process characteristics determine that?
unit_of_decision: One source-to-target transfer decision (a project pair)
human_role: Analyst deciding whether to reuse a foreign predictor
when_human_is_involved: Before reuse, at the transfer decision
judgment_representation: A fitted statistical prediction model, not a judgment record
scope_captured: PARTIAL - transfer validity characterised per project pair
provenance: PARTIAL - the source project of each predictor is recorded
reuse_supported: YES - reuse of a source predictor in a target project is the object of study
target_context_checked: YES - transfer is assessed against the target project's own characteristics
independent_target_evidence: YES - measured against independent labelled outcomes in the target project
local_vs_transferable_failure_classifica: PARTIAL - determines empirically whether a predictive relationship is project-local or transfers, but does not attribute a recurring correction to a pipeline limitation versus a local cause
evaluation_type: Large-scale controlled empirical experiment over many source-target pairs
dataset: Industrial and open-source projects yielding several hundred cross-project prediction pairs
metrics: Precision, recall and accuracy thresholds for transfer success
main_result: Cross-project transfer succeeded in only a small fraction of the tested pairs; transfer success depends systematically on data, domain and process characteristics rather than on similarity of domain alone.
exact_gap_effect: The strongest challenge to GAP-3's methodological novelty. Empirical, target-evidence-based transfer testing per source-target pair is established software-engineering practice. GAP-3's residual must be located in the unit (one recorded human judgment, one reuse event) and in the joint similarity, applicability, authorisation, currency and benefit test.
limitations: The transferred object is a fitted model over labelled defect data, not one expert's judgment about one contested claim; no authorisation, validity or benefit gate on the individual reuse event.

full_citation: B. Turhan, T. Menzies, A. B. Bener, J. Di Stefano, 'On the relative value of cross-company and within-company data for defect prediction', Empirical Software Engineering 14(5), pp. 540-578, 2009.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on transfer with target evidence; Crossref verification
research_problem: Is foreign, cross-company defect data useful when local data are scarce, and can irrelevant foreign data be filtered before use?
unit_of_decision: One reuse decision over foreign training data
human_role: Analyst deciding whether and how to admit foreign data
when_human_is_involved: Before reuse
judgment_representation: Training instances and fitted predictors
target_context_checked: YES - nearest-neighbour relevancy filtering selects foreign instances similar to the target context
independent_target_evidence: YES - evaluated against the target project's own defect outcomes
evaluation_type: Controlled empirical comparison
dataset: NASA MDP and Turkish software company datasets
baseline: Within-company models and unfiltered cross-company models
metrics: Probability of detection, probability of false alarm, balance
main_result: Unfiltered cross-company data inflate false alarms; nearest-neighbour relevancy filtering of foreign data makes cross-company prediction competitive with within-company models when local data are scarce.
exact_gap_effect: Establishes similarity-plus-applicability filtering of foreign experience before it is allowed to act, validated against target outcomes. Reinforces the G3-01 narrowing of GAP-3.
limitations: Filtering is feature-space similarity only; no authorisation, currency or authority; no per-judgment decision; no explicit quirk-versus-capability-gap classification.

full_citation: B. Chen, J. Tackman, M. Setala, T. Poranen, Z. Zhang, 'Integrating Access Control with Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Proof of Concept for Managing Sensitive Patient Profiles', Proc. 40th ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC 2025), pp. 915-919, 2025.
peer_review_status: Tier B - peer-reviewed conference short paper

human_role: Requesting user whose entitlements determine what may be retrieved
when_human_is_involved: At query time, as the subject of the authorisation decision
authority_modelled: PARTIAL - subject entitlement to read an object, not authority to decide
judgment_representation: not_applicable
revocation: PARTIAL - permission changes take effect at retrieval

reuse_scope: Within the governed corpus, filtered by the requester's permissions

full_citation: R. Weber, D. W. Aha, I. Becerra-Fernandez, 'Intelligent lessons learned systems', Expert Systems with Applications 20(1), pp. 17-34, 2001.
discovery_source: Adjacent-literature search on organisational and case memory; Crossref verification

human_role: Lesson author, verifier, and later decision maker who may apply the lesson
when_human_is_involved: At collection, verification, storage, dissemination and application
authority_modelled: PARTIAL - verification implies an approving role, but authority is not modelled

scope_captured: PARTIAL - applicability context is described in prose, not enforced

metrics: Qualitative assessment of system architecture and use

limitations: Provenance informs store competence and confidence; it does not decide whether one stored judgment may act in one specific later context under someone's authority, and applies no authorisation, currency or target-evidence test.

full_citation: P. Runeson, M. Alexandersson, O. Nyholm, 'Detection of Duplicate Defect Reports Using Natural Language Processing', Proc. 29th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2007), pp. 499-510, 2007.

full_citation: J. Fugener, J. Grahl, A. Gupta, W. Ketter, 'Cognitive Challenges in Human-Artificial Intelligence Collaboration: Investigating the Path Toward Productive Delegation', Information Systems Research 33(2), pp. 678-696, 2022.

human_role: Delegator and performer
when_human_is_involved: At the delegation decision and at task performance
who_is_selected: Either the human or the AI
competence_modelled: YES - relative competence of human and AI, empirically measured
authority_modelled: PARTIAL - who holds the delegation right is the experimental manipulation, not a modelled construct
